sections.skill: Explain overdrafts and compute the cost of overdraft and related fees

questions.prompt: What is an overdraft?

choices.text: Taking out a loan with a fixed monthly payment
Keeping a balance above the minimum required
Transferring money from checking to savings
Spending more than the account holds

questions.correct_answer: Spending more than the account holds
questions.intro: An overdraft happens when a payment or purchase is larger than the money in the account and the bank pays it anyway. The account goes negative, and the bank may charge an overdraft fee. If the bank refuses the payment instead, the item is returned unpaid, and a returned-item ("NSF") fee may apply.
questions.feedback: An overdraft means the account was overdrawn: the balance went below zero.

misconceptions.A: Confuses an overdraft with an installment loan
misconceptions.C: Confuses an overdraft with a transfer

sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Mason's balance is $30. His bank charges $35 per overdraft. He makes three debit card purchases: $12, then $25, then $8, and he has opted in to overdraft coverage. If each purchase that makes the balance negative (or more negative) gets a fee, how much will he pay in fees?
questions.intro: Each item paid while the account is overdrawn can trigger its own fee. Track the balance item by item. A small purchase can cost far more than its price once a fee is added.
questions.feedback: $30 − $12 = $18 (no fee). $18 − $25 = −$7 (fee). −$7 − $8 = −$15 (fee). Two fees: 2 × $35 = $70. Counting the fees, his balance ends at −$15 − $70 = −$85.

misconceptions.D: Charges a fee on every purchase
misconceptions.A: Uses the amount overdrawn as the fee

sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Without opting in to overdraft coverage, what usually happens when Leah tries a one-time debit card purchase larger than her balance?

choices.text: The purchase is declined, with no overdraft fee
The purchase is approved, and she pays a $35 fee
The store gives her the item for free
Her account is closed immediately

questions.correct_answer: The purchase is declined, with no overdraft fee
questions.intro: Federal rules say a bank must get your permission (your "opt-in") before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases. If you do not opt in, those transactions are usually declined. Checks and automatic bill payments are treated differently and can still be overdrawn.
questions.feedback: Without opt-in, one-time debit purchases above the balance are usually declined, so no overdraft fee applies.

misconceptions.C: Thinks the store absorbs the shortfall

sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Hana links her savings account to checking for overdraft protection. The bank charges $10 per automatic transfer instead of a $35 overdraft fee. She overdraws twice this month. How much does linking save her this month?
questions.intro: Overdraft protection links checking to another account, such as savings or a line of credit. When checking runs short, money is moved automatically to cover the item. Banks often charge a transfer fee, but it is usually smaller than an overdraft fee.

misconceptions.A: Gives the transfer fees instead of the savings

sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Ray's $80 electric bill payment is returned unpaid because his account is short. Which result is MOST likely?

choices.text: He may owe a returned-item fee, and the bill is still unpaid
The bill is paid, and no one charges any fee
The electric company cancels the bill
His bank pays the bill from its own funds and never charges him for it

questions.correct_answer: He may owe a returned-item fee, and the bill is still unpaid
questions.feedback: A returned (NSF) payment can cost a bank fee and a late fee from the biller, and the bill remains due.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a returned payment still counts
misconceptions.C: Thinks a failed payment erases the debt
misconceptions.D: Thinks the bank pays at no cost

sections.relationship: Students must understand a negative balance as money owed before they can reason about overdraft fees.

questions.prompt: Rina's balance is $20. She spends $26. If the bank pays it, what is her balance (before any fee)?
questions.intro: When spending is larger than the balance and the bank pays anyway, the balance becomes negative. A negative balance means you owe the bank that amount.

misconceptions.B: Thinks the bank stops at zero

questions.prompt: What does a balance of −$6 mean?

choices.text: The bank owes Rina $6
Rina has $6 left to spend
The account has been closed
Rina owes the bank $6

questions.intro: A negative account balance is a debt to the bank. You must deposit enough to bring the balance back to zero or above.
questions.feedback: A negative balance is money owed to the bank.

misconceptions.C: Thinks a negative balance closes the account

questions.prompt: Rina's balance is −$6, and the bank adds a $35 overdraft fee. What is her new balance?
questions.intro: A fee is subtracted from the balance, even when the balance is already negative, which makes it more negative.

misconceptions.D: Adds the fee to a positive 6
misconceptions.C: Subtracts 6 from 35 and keeps the sign

questions.feedback: She must deposit $41 to cover both the shortfall and the fee.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a negative balance resets itself

questions.prompt: Rina had $20 available in checking and made a $26 debit purchase, overdrawing her account. Which choice would have prevented this?

choices.text: Making the purchase on a different day of the week instead
Using the card at a larger store
Checking her balance the day after the purchase
Checking her available balance and skipping or shrinking the purchase

questions.correct_answer: Checking her available balance and skipping or shrinking the purchase
questions.intro: The available balance already subtracts pending transactions. Checking it helps only if you then act on it: wait, spend less, or add cleared money first.
questions.feedback: Knowing the available balance ($20) and then waiting or buying less (or adding cleared funds first) prevents the overdraft.

misconceptions.C: Checks too late to prevent the overdraft

sections.skill: The yearly cost of fee habits

questions.prompt: Jae overdraws his account exactly once every month for a year and pays a $34 fee each time. How much do the fees cost him in that year?
questions.intro: A habit that causes a fee every month becomes a large yearly cost. Multiply the monthly cost by 12 to see the yearly impact.
sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Jae pays a $34 overdraft fee about once a month, each time on a $9 debit purchase. What does each of those purchases really cost?
questions.intro: When a purchase overdraws the account, its true cost is the purchase price plus the overdraft fee.

misconceptions.B: Subtracts the purchase from the fee

sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Jae overdraws about once a month because he buys things without checking his balance. Which step would MOST directly prevent his overdrafts?

choices.text: Use a different debit card from the same account
Make purchases late at night
Ask the bank for paper statements instead of e-statements
Set a low-balance alert and keep a small buffer in checking

questions.correct_answer: Set a low-balance alert and keep a small buffer in checking
questions.intro: Low-balance alerts warn you before you overspend. A buffer, a small amount you treat as untouchable, absorbs timing surprises such as a bill that posts a day early.
questions.feedback: Alerts plus a buffer address the cause: spending without knowing the balance.

misconceptions.A: The account is still the same
misconceptions.C: Statements arrive too late to prevent them

sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Jae pays $408 a year in overdraft fees (12 × $34). Keeping a $100 buffer, money he leaves in checking and never spends, would have prevented all 12 overdrafts. Compare keeping the buffer with paying the fees.

choices.text: The buffer saves $408 and stays his money
The buffer costs him $100 per month
The buffer and the fees cost the same
The buffer saves $100 and costs $408

questions.correct_answer: The buffer saves $408 and stays his money
questions.feedback: The buffer remains in his account, while fees are gone forever.

misconceptions.C: Treats money kept as money lost

questions.prompt: Some banks have reduced or ended overdraft fees, and others still charge them. What is the best way to learn your own bank's current policy?

choices.text: Read the current fee schedule or ask the bank directly
Assume every bank charges exactly $35
Assume overdraft fees are banned everywhere
Rely on what a friend's bank charged for overdrafts five years ago

questions.correct_answer: Read the current fee schedule or ask the bank directly
questions.feedback: Overdraft policies differ by bank and change over time; the current fee schedule is the authority.

sections.skill: Linked accounts and overdraft lines of credit

questions.prompt: An overdraft line of credit covers shortfalls with a loan that charges 18% interest (APR 18%; no other finance charges). Kim borrows $200 through it and repays it after one month. About how much interest does she pay (simple interest for 1/12 of a year)?
questions.intro: An overdraft line of credit is a small loan account linked to checking. When checking runs short, it lends the difference, and you pay interest (and sometimes a fee) until you repay it. Interest for part of a year ≈ principal × annual rate × fraction of a year.
sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Kim compares two ways to cover a $200 shortfall for one month: a $35 overdraft fee, or about $3 of interest plus a $5 transfer fee on her line of credit. Which costs less and by how much?

choices.text: The overdraft fee, by $27
The line of credit, by $32
They cost the same
The line of credit, by $27

sources: CFPB: Banks must get the customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases; checks and recurring payments may be paid into overdraft without that opt-in. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-overdraft-coverage-en-1015/)

questions.prompt: Which risk applies to an overdraft line of credit but NOT to a savings-linked transfer?

choices.text: Unpaid amounts keep collecting interest
It moves your own savings into checking
It can never be used more than once
It is covered by FDIC insurance if unpaid

questions.feedback: A line of credit is a loan; a savings link moves your own money.

questions.prompt: Which account would a bank usually check before approving an overdraft line of credit?

choices.text: Your school transcript
Nothing, since it is part of a checking account you already have
Your savings account interest rate
Your credit history, because it is a loan

questions.correct_answer: Your credit history, because it is a loan
questions.feedback: Because a line of credit is lending, the bank reviews your creditworthiness.

misconceptions.C: Confuses deposit terms with credit approval
